My observations and thoughts:
The Round 2 result is decisive. Dropping price from $3.50 → $2.50 (a 29% cut) raised quantity from 0.25 → 10.65 (a ~43× increase), and profit from $0.62 → $15.98. Demand is highly elastic in this range, so the optimum is almost certainly below $2.50. The competitor matched us again, so cross-price effects are muted/parallel — we're effectively competing on the same demand curve.

I can now estimate elasticity from two points (linear demand assumption). Using (p, q): (3.50, 0.25) and (2.50, 10.65). Slope = (10.65 − 0.25)/(2.50 − 3.50) = 10.4 / (−1) = −10.4 units per $1. Demand: q = 10.65 − 10.4(p − 2.50) = 36.65 − 10.4p. Intercept at q=0: p = 3.524. Check max WTP $4.51 — demand already hits zero at ~$3.52, consistent with weak high-end sales.

Profit = (p − 1)(36.65 − 10.4p). Expand: 36.65p − 10.4p² − 36.65 + 10.4p = −10.4p² + 47.05p − 36.65. Vertex: p = 47.05/(2×10.4) = 47.05/20.8 ≈ $2.26. So the linear-model optimum is ~$2.26.

Caveat: two points only, and the huge jump may partly reflect a nonlinear/threshold demand curve, not a straight line. If demand is convex (very price-sensitive near $2.50–$3.50 but flattening lower), the true optimum could be a bit lower; if the linear fit overstates sensitivity at low prices, optimum could be a bit higher. So I should probe one point just below the estimate (e.g., $2.00) and one just above (e.g., $2.75) to bracket the optimum and refine the curve. Next round: test ~$2.00 to see if quantity continues rising strongly (optimum lower) or flattens/reverses (optimum near $2.26–$2.50).
